title: Next month I'll go to Jaipur
title_target: मैं जयपुर जाऊँगी — maiⁿ jaypur jaauuⁿgii
goal: Talk about plans and the weather — and enjoy one piece of good news: the future never takes ने, even when the verb has an object.
bekal: talking about weather and seasons in India

dialogs.title: संवाद — When to go to Jaipur
dialogs.intro: Rahul advises Ani on the best time to travel. Notice something reassuring: every past sentence in Unit 14 used ने, but not a single future sentence on this page does.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: What are you doing next month?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Next month? It'll be really hot.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: It can go up to forty-five degrees.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Oh no! In Indonesia even thirty-two feels like a lot.
lines.literal: oh-no! Indonesia — in — thirty-two — even — a-lot — is.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Then go in July. There'll be rain, and the weather will be nice.
lines.literal: then — July — in — go. rain — will-be(fem.), weather — good — will-stay.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Won't it be hard to get around in the rain?
lines.literal: rain — in — getting-around — hard — not — will-be?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: A little. But the first rain of the monsoon — that's something else.
lines.literal: a-little. but — monsoon — of(fem.) — first(fem.) — rain — that — something — else — just — is.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: The whole city comes outside. When you see it, you'll understand.
lines.literal: whole — city — outside — come-out — comes — is. you — will-see(fem.) — then — will-understand(fem.).

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: All right, I'll go in July.

notes: **The future: stem + ऊँ/ए/ओ/एँ + गा · गी · गे.** The first part shows the subject; the **-गा/-गी/-गे** part shows gender and number. *मैं जा**ऊँगा*** (male), *मैं जा**ऊँगी*** (female), *वह जा**एगा***, *हम जा**एँगे***, *तुम जा**ओगे***.

**⚠️ And here's the good news: ने never appears in the future.** *मैं**ने** खाना खाया* (past, with ने) but ***मैं** खाना खाऊँगी* (future, no ने). The ने ending lives only in past sentences. So if you're not yet comfortable with Unit 14, you can still talk freely about plans — and that isn't cheating, it's just how the language works.

**The verb goes back to agreeing with the subject.** *मैं चाय पीऊँगी* — पीऊँगी is feminine because **I** am female, not because चाय is feminine. The future behaves like the habitual in Unit 4, not like the past in Unit 14.

**होगा has two meanings, both very common.** First, "will be": *कल बारिश **होगी*** (it will rain tomorrow). Second, **a guess about now**: *वे घर पर **होंगे*** (he's probably at home). ⚠️ The second meaning is very common in conversation and often confuses beginners. The time word decides: with *कल* → future; no time word → a guess. (English does something similar: "that'll be the postman".)

**तो means "then" when it links two clauses.** *आप देखेंगी **तो** समझेंगी* — "if you see it, then you'll understand". The full form uses **अगर … तो …** (*अगर बारिश हुई तो हम नहीं जाएँगे*), but in conversation the अगर is often dropped and the तो stays. This is a different तो from the emphatic तो in Unit 3 — context tells them apart.

**कुछ और ही है — a small, very Hindi phrase.** Literally "it's just something else", meaning "it's special, it's in a class of its own". You'll hear it about food, music, places and people: *उनकी बात ही कुछ और है*. One short phrase that makes your praise sound sincere.

**About the first monsoon rain — Rahul isn't exaggerating.** The arrival of the monsoon after weeks of forty-degree heat is a truly celebrated event in India: people pour outside, children play in the rain, sellers of **पकौड़े** (fritters) appear on every corner, and songs about बारिश play everywhere. ⚠️ If you get the chance to be in India in late June or early July, don't hide in your room that day.

grammars.title: The future

head: Sentence
Form
Note
rows: ⚠️ has an object, but still no ने
If it rains, we won't go.
अगर बारिश हुई तो हम नहीं जाएँगे।

after: ⚠️ **लेना → लूँगा/लूँगी**, **देना → दूँगा/दूँगी**, **पीना → पिऊँगा/पिऊँगी**, **होना → होऊँगा** (rare) or more often **हूँगा**. These four bend the pattern a little; the rest are regular.

grammars.title: Weather and seasons
after: Everyday weather sentences: **आज बहुत गरमी है** (it's very hot today), **बारिश हो रही है** (it's raining), **मौसम अच्छा है** (the weather is nice), **कल बारिश होगी** (it'll rain tomorrow), **बहुत उमस है** (it's really muggy). ⚠️ Note that rain **happens** (होना), it doesn't **fall**: *बारिश हो रही है*, not *बारिश गिर रही है*.

blocks.text: India has far more distinct seasons than many travelers expect, and when you visit shapes your whole experience. This table is knowledge people usually only gain after picking the wrong month once.

head: Months
Season
What usually happens
rows: The most comfortable time to travel; in the north it can get very cold, close to zero at night.
Still bearable; flowers bloom in the north.
⚠️ Forty to forty-five degrees on the northern plains. Avoid if you can.
Heavy rain on and off, green everywhere, prices drop; ⚠️ road travel can be disrupted.
The weather improves, and the festival season begins — Dussehra and Diwali.

blocks.title: Sentences for talking about plans
items: **मैं अगले महीने जयपुर जाऊँगी।** — Next month I'll go to Jaipur.
**मैं तीन दिन रुकूँगी।** — I'll stay three days.
**हम ट्रेन से जाएँगे।** — We'll go by train.
**अगर मौसम अच्छा रहा तो हम घूमेंगे।** — If the weather's nice, we'll go sightseeing.
**मैं आपको फ़ोन करूँगी।** — I'll call you.
**देखते हैं।** — We'll see. ⚠️ A very useful answer when you don't want to decide yet — and one Indians use constantly.

blocks.text: A note about **देखते हैं**. Literally "we see", it's one of the most typical phrases in Indian conversation: used to put off a decision without refusing, to answer an invitation that isn't settled yet, and sometimes to say "no" in a way that doesn't hurt. ⚠️ If you invite someone and they answer *देखते हैं*, don't assume it means "yes". Unit 19 covers the whole art of declining politely, which in India is done almost without ever saying the word "no".
